\chapter{Hablando --- An Action Caught in the Middle}
\label{ch:hablando}
\hlchaptermodality{236}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can form the -ando shape of an -ar verb.}

I can form the -ando shape of an -ar verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablando]{hablando — an action caught in the middle}

\label{lesson:ES-C62-hablando}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hablo} says that I speak. It does not say I am speaking \textbf{right now}, this minute, with my mouth open.

Spanish has a separate form for that, and it is built from the infinitive.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: swap the ending}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{habl-} \textbf{ar} $\to$ \emph{habl-} \emph{\textbf{ando}}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{hablar} & \emph{\textbf{hablando}} \\
\emph{trabajar} & \emph{\textbf{trabajando}} \\
\emph{estudiar} & \emph{\textbf{estudiando}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Take the \emph{-ar} off, put \emph{-ando} on. There is nothing to agree with and nothing to conjugate: \textbf{one form, for everybody}. After all the endings this book has asked you to learn, that is a holiday.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin had a form for an action thought of as a \textbf{thing being done} — the \emph{gerund}, ending in \emph{-ndum}. Spanish kept the ending almost untouched and threw away everything else about it: Latin's gerund had case endings, and Spanish's has none at all.

What survives is the meaning: not \emph{to speak}, not \emph{I speak}, but \textbf{speaking} — the action underway, with no beginning and no end attached.

English built its \emph{-ing} separately and lands in almost the same place, which is why \emph{hablando} feels immediately familiar. Almost. The two part company later, and this book will show you where.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hablando}, \emph{trabajando}, \emph{estudiando}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What replaces the \emph{-ar}? (\emph{\textbf{-ando}}.)

And how many endings does this form have? (\textbf{One.} It agrees with nothing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
